articles.title: Mother’s feeding practices may influence children’s reluctance to try new foods: NIN study
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Food neophobia among children can limit dietary variety and potentially affect nutritional health during crucial years of growth

A mother’s knowledge, attitude and feeding practices can significantly influence a child’s willingness to try new foods , which highlights the need for stronger nutrition counselling for caregivers during early childhood, according to a new study by researchers at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).

The study, published in the Journal of Nutritional Science , examined food neophobia, a condition in which children are reluctant to try unfamiliar or diverse foods. Such behaviour can limit dietary variety and potentially affect nutritional health during crucial years of growth.

Researchers assessed 150 mother-child pairs from Addagutta in Hyderabad between August and October 2025 focusing on children aged two- seven years and explored how maternal feeding practices were associated with food neophobia and children’s nutritional status.

The findings revealed that nearly 77% of children showed moderate levels of food neophobia, while 11.3% displayed high levels and 12% had low levels. Boys recorded slightly higher food neophobia scores than girls, although the differences were not statistically significant.

The study also found a link between nutritional status and food acceptance. Children suffering from wasting were more likely to exhibit higher food neophobia scores than those with normal nutritional status, suggesting that reluctance to try new foods may be associated with poorer dietary outcomes.

Researchers observed that maternal knowledge, attitudes and practices played an important role. Children whose mothers demonstrated moderate levels of nutrition-related knowledge and positive feeding practices had lower food neophobia scores than those whose mothers had lower scores.

Karthikeyan Ramanujam, Scientist-C at ICMR-NIN and lead author of the study, said the findings underscore the importance of everyday feeding behaviours. He suggested that caregivers should repeatedly offer a variety of foods without pressure, create positive mealtime experiences and respond supportively when children reject unfamiliar foods.

ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings offer an opportunity to strengthen behavioural feeding counselling through existing government programmes such as the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) and POSHAN Abhiyaan.

Researchers cautioned that the study was limited to a single urban low-income community and a relatively small sample size. They noted that, as a cross-sectional study, it identifies associations but cannot establish direct cause-and-effect relationships, as per a press release.

articles.title: Keralam Assembly: Orders issued to procure 2,159 bottles of SMA drug, says Health Minister
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Replying to a submission, Minister says government is taking several steps through Kerala United Against Rare Diseases scheme to provide timely treatment and life-saving medicines to children affected by SMA

The Kerala government has issued orders for procuring 2,159 bottles of Risdiplam , the first at-home, oral treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), to ensure continued availability of the medicine, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan has said.

Replying to a submission by P.K. Firos, MLA, in the Assembly on Thursday, the Minister said the government was taking several steps through the KARE (Kerala United Against Rare Diseases) scheme to provide timely treatment and life-saving medicines to children affected by SMA, a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function.
Medicines and related treatment were made available through the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, he said.

Keralam used to obtain Risdiplam, under its trade name, at a negotiated price of ₹5.5 lakh per bottle. Since October 19, it had been providing a less expensive generic version of the drug manufactured in the country by Natco Pharma. The drug Natsmart cost only around ₹11,000, significantly bringing down treatment costs and making the medicine available to more children.
Besides medicines, the government also provided physiotherapy, respiratory therapy, respiratory devices, rehabilitation, and surgery, the Minister said.
Keralam has been providing Risdiplam free of cost to children under 12 since 2022 through KARE. Steps have been taken to provide all eligible persons the medicine lifelong, he said.

Referring to two children of a couple who had registered with the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital on October 6 and had Type 2 SMA, the Minister said they were eligible for free Risdiplam. Urgent steps were being taken to provide them with treatment the approval of a technical experts committee. Natsmart was being provided to them. Medicines and treatment would be provided to the couple’s third child through KARE on completion of check-up, he added.

The government would also consider devising more comprehensive programmes in association with the Kerala Social Security Mission to provide treatment and financial and psychological support to the affected children and their families. The government, the Minister said, was committed to ensuring that treatment was not disrupted, medicines were available continuously, and the financial burden on families was reduced.

Replying to a submission, Minister says government is taking several steps through Kerala United Against Rare Diseases scheme to provide timely treatment and life-saving medicines to children affected by SMA

The Kerala government has issued orders for procuring 2,159 bottles of Risdiplam , the first at-home, oral treatment for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), to ensure continued availability of the medicine, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan has said.

Replying to a submission by P.K. Firos, MLA, in the Assembly on Thursday, the Minister said the government was taking several steps through the KARE (Kerala United Against Rare Diseases) scheme to provide timely treatment and life-saving medicines to children affected by SMA, a rare, life-threatening genetic disorder that progressively weakens muscles, severely impairing both mobility and respiratory function.

Medicines and related treatment were made available through the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, he said.

Keralam used to obtain Risdiplam, under its trade name, at a negotiated price of ₹5.5 lakh per bottle. Since October 19, it had been providing a less expensive generic version of the drug manufactured in the country by Natco Pharma. The drug Natsmart cost only around ₹11,000, significantly bringing down treatment costs and making the medicine available to more children.

Besides medicines, the government also provided physiotherapy, respiratory therapy, respiratory devices, rehabilitation, and surgery, the Minister said.

Keralam has been providing Risdiplam free of cost to children under 12 since 2022 through KARE. Steps have been taken to provide all eligible persons the medicine lifelong, he said.

Referring to two children of a couple who had registered with the SMA clinic at SAT Hospital on October 6 and had Type 2 SMA, the Minister said they were eligible for free Risdiplam. Urgent steps were being taken to provide them with treatment the approval of a technical experts committee. Natsmart was being provided to them. Medicines and treatment would be provided to the couple’s third child through KARE on completion of check-up, he added.

The government would also consider devising more comprehensive programmes in association with the Kerala Social Security Mission to provide treatment and financial and psychological support to the affected children and their families. The government, the Minister said, was committed to ensuring that treatment was not disrupted, medicines were available continuously, and the financial burden on families was reduced.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: The government would also consider devising more comprehensive programmes in association with the Kerala Social Security Mission to provide treatment and financial and psychological support to the affected children and their families. articles.title: Deepavali sales expected to gain momentum in Coimbatore next week
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: With Deepavali falling in the first week of a month this year, people are likely to begin shopping after receiving their monthly salaries and festival bonuses; the last 5-6 days preceding the festival is likely to witness massive retail activity
Shopping for the Deepavali festival in Coimbatore city this year is expected to pick up next week across sectors.
President of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Coimbatore, C. Dorairaj, told The Hindu on Thursday (October 29) that several companies in Coimbatore will disburse bonuses next week.

With the festival coming in the first week of a month this year, people are likely to start purchases after getting the monthly salary and the festival bonus. So, the last 5-6 days preceding the festival is expected to see huge retail activity.
Be it textiles, FMCG, or household appliances, the retailers are expecting good sales this year.

All the products have seen a price hike, ranging between 10% and 30%, in the last few months, depending on the product. So, the retailers may see higher revenue though the volume of sales may remain the same as last year or slightly better in some sectors, he added.

In the case of textiles, while the large, multi brand retail outlets are already witnessing a pick up of sales, the smaller outlets are facing stiff competition from online sellers. Further, business at the small retail shops will go up in the last few days before the festival.

Though gold and silver prices saw a decline recently, jewellery retailers are yet to see business picking up. “We were hoping for better sales as the prices fell. But, consumers are waiting for further fall in prices,” said B. Sabarinath, president of the Coimbatore Jewellers Association.
The household appliances outlets are also expecting better sales only from next week.
In the case of sweets and savouries, most of the bulk buyers will purchase products for distribution just days before the festival, Mr. Dorairaj said.

articles.title: India votes in favour of UNGA resolution calling for end to US embargo on Cuba
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The 193-member General Assembly adopted the resolution on October 28, with 130 countries voting in favour, 17 against and 25 abstaining

India voted in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution calling for an end to the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the U.S. against Cuba, reiterating that the restrictions should be lifted to help the Caribbean nation pursue its development aspirations.
The 193-member General Assembly adopted the resolution on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) with 130 countries voting in favour, 17 against and 25 abstaining.

Delivering India's statement, Counsellor at India's Permanent Mission to the UN Soumya Nair said the General Assembly has repeatedly called for an end to the embargo and rejected laws and regulations with extraterritorial effects that adversely affect the sovereignty of other states and the progress and prosperity of their peoples.

"India reiterates the Assembly's call to all states to refrain from promulgating and applying, and to repeal and invalidate, such laws and measures in conformity with their obligations under the Charter of the United Nations and international law," she said.
Ms. Nair said India's commitment to multilateralism is rooted in the belief that international challenges are best addressed through dialogue and diplomacy, in accordance with the UN Charter.

"It is in this spirit that India hopes that the embargo will be lifted at the earliest to help create an environment that would enable the people of Cuba to participate more fully in international cooperation and pursue their legitimate development aspirations,” she said.
Citing a report by the UN Secretary-General, Ms. Nair highlighted the impact of the restrictions on Cuba's economy and essential services.
Cuba's health system faces shortages of over 60% of essential medicines, while food production has declined by more than 50% in the past five years, she said.

“The restrictions on fuel exports to Cuba have also aggravated the country's ongoing energy crisis. The shortages have disrupted essential services, including healthcare, education, water supplies, food distribution, and transportation,” Ms. Nair said.

The conflict between America and Cuba stems from a decades-old political, economic, and ideological divide that began when Fidel Castro overthrew a U.S.-backed government in 1959 and aligned the island with the Soviet Union.

articles.title: Iran says four tankers on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The vessels had "switched off all their radar and navigation systems" and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said

At least four tankers have caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to navigate the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's armed forces said on Thursday (October 29, 2026), a day after the U.S. military said it had cleared key routes through the waterway.

"Over the past 24 hours, three violating oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking mines while attempting to pass through the unauthorised southern route of the Strait of Hormuz," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement.
The vessels had "switched off all their radar and navigation systems" and disregarded warnings from the IRGC navy, the statement said.
It was not immediately clear when the incidents occurred or which flags the tankers were flying.
Later on Thursday (October 29, 2026), Iran's army reported that another tanker had caught fire east of the strait.

"A tanker that was illegally operating in a restricted and dangerous area east of the Strait of Hormuz was damaged and caught fire after striking naval mines, rendering it unable to move," the army said in a statement carried by State television.

In recent weeks, Iran has reported multiple vessels striking sea mines, prompting U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), which runs military operations in the region, to reaffirm on social media its insistence that all mines in "primary transit routes" have been cleared.

On Thursday (October 29, 2026), Hossein Mohebi, the spokesman for the IRGC challenged the claim, saying, "Prove your Hormuz mine-clearing claim with independent evidence, not statements!" in a post on X.
Since the outbreak of the war on February 28, Iran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil and gas consumption.

The United States has in response imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait. On Sunday (October 25, 2026), CENTCOM said it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.

articles.title: Serbia’s students demand resignations in police, judiciary as they prepare to take power
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The Students’ List movement swept the parliamentary election on October 25, 2026 against Vucic’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, which has ruled unchallenged for 14 years

Serbia 's student movement on Thursday (October 29, 2026) demanded the resignations of top officials in the police, intelligence agencies, and the judiciary as they prepare to take power after a historic election win last weekend against former strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic.

The students at a news conference also urged Serbia's election authorities to officially declare the final results of Sunday's (October 25, 2026) ballot without delay after a rerun at some 50 polling stations next Sunday (November 1, 2026), so that a new Parliament and government can be formed.

The Students’ List movement swept the parliamentary election on Sunday (October 25, 2026) against Mr. Vucic’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, which has ruled unchallenged for 14 years. The outgoing authorities remain in control as the formal transition of power will take several weeks.

“Changes are starting now,” student Filip Ubovic said at the news conference held at a central Belgrade park that used to be a sealed-off area occupied by Mr. Vucic's loyalists. “Institutions belong to the citizens and the law applies to everyone.”

Mr. Vucic's party has gradually taken control over all State institutions since it came to power in 2012. The SNS party has been accused of rampant corruption and cronyism, links to organised crime, and pressure on the judiciary, police, and the media, which the populists have denied.
The students on Thursday (October 29, 2026) asked public servants to prevent outgoing officials from destroying documentation or evidence of potential wrongdoing.

Mr. Vucic on Thursday (October 29, 2026) held a news conference of his own, accusing the election winners of “revolutionary terror" after groups of people stormed the Informer TV station that led the pre-election propaganda branding the students as traitors and enemies of the State.

Suspicions of State corruption in infrastructure projects two years ago set off a wave of street protests after a collapsed canopy at a train station in Serbia's north killed 16 people after a renovation. The students led those protests before challenging and defeating Mr. Vucic at the early ballot on Sunday (October 25, 2026).

The students' win on Sunday (October 25, 2026) marks the first time that a grassroot youth movement toppled a well-established political leader. It comes at the moment when similar movements are mushrooming across Europe.

The students said in their briefing that top police officials and the intelligence agencies had served Mr. Vucic's party during the protests in violation of the law. They have been accused of using excessive force against protesters, illegal surveillance, detention and pressure on Mr. Vucic's political opponents.

articles.title: Experts warn of wider spread as Ebola outbreak reaches plateau
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A major challenge in Congo is limited contact tracing and collaboration with affected communities; health workers sometimes spend more time trying to convince locals to work with them than giving care
The Ebola outbreak in Congo passed a grim milestone this week — 10,000 confirmed cases — and spurred questions about whether health authorities are losing their ability to contain it.

Nearly half the infected people in this outbreak have died, and some experts say there are reasons to worry this could grow into the worst Ebola outbreak in history. Others don't think it will reach that level. Researchers are currently working on updated projections.

Current circumstances suggest it's unlikely to spark significant problems in most other countries, some researchers said. But about 30 confirmed cases have already popped up in other nations. And the risk that more will appear outside Congo will grow if the outbreak isn't tamed, said Justin Lessler, a University of North Carolina researcher who studies the dynamics of infectious disease outbreaks.
Experts also are hopeful that a vaccine will become available next year that could help control it.

At a virtual summit of African health ministers on Wednesday, Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya said the continent is “not winning” the fight against Ebola and needs to do more after it spread to multiple African countries. “Together, we agreed to prepare every country, coordinate across our borders and keep those borders open while watching them closely,” Kaseya wrote on X.
Steady case numbers raise concerns about spread beyond Congo

About 400 to 500 new confirmed cases have been reported in Congo each week, and that number seems to be holding steady. It's good news that “cases are not rising exponentially,” at least for the moment, said Dr. Boghuma Titanji, an Emory University infectious disease specialist.
“But they're not coming down, either," she said. "It's at a plateau. And the plateau is at a very, very high set point."

A major challenge in Congo is limited contact tracing and collaboration with affected communities; health workers sometimes spend more time trying to convince locals to work with them than giving care.

Fewer than a quarter of new cases are coming from people known to have been in contact with an infected person, showing there are ongoing chains of transmission that health authorities are not aware of.

articles.title: ICMR funds study to identify genetic links, potential therapies for autoimmune diseases
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The findings could help scientists better understand the disease processes involved and identify potential targets for developing new therapies

The Indian Council of Medical Research has funded a four-year study to investigate the genetic and immunological mechanisms underlying autoimmune diseases by studying families with multiple affected members, AIIMS doctors said on Thursday, appealing to SLE patients to get enrolled in the study.

The project titled ‘Genomic Profiling and Identification of Targetable Shared Immunopathogenic Events in Multiplex Families with Autoimmune Diseases’ has been awarded to Dipyaman Ganguly of Ashoka University, Sonipat, Haryana, and Ranjan Gupta, additional professor in the Department of Rheumatology, AIIMS, Delhi.

The study aims to build a nationwide cohort of 200 families in which multiple members are affected by autoimmune diseases. Each participating family must have at least one member diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), commonly known as lupus, Gupta said.

The researchers will conduct genetic and immunological assessments of the enrolled patients and their family members to identify shared biological mechanisms that contribute to the development of these conditions.
The findings could help scientists better understand the disease processes involved and identify potential targets for developing new therapies, he said.

Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. A family history of such conditions is associated with an increased risk of developing them, highlighting the importance of investigating genetic and shared immunological factors, Gupta said.

The four-year project will involve clinical centres at AIIMS Delhi; AIIMS Bibinagar, Telangana; Sanjay Gandhi Postgraduate Institute of Medical Sciences (SGPGIMS), Lucknow; St John's Hospital, Bengaluru; Nizam's Institute of Medical Sciences, Hyderabad; and the Kolkata Medical College. These centres will contribute clinical data and biological samples for the study.
Patients diagnosed with lupus and residing in Delhi-NCR can contact the centre at AIIMS Delhi to check their eligibility for participation, Gupta said.
Participation will be subject to eligibility assessment and the study's enrolment requirements.

articles.title: Heat-related deaths up 36% since Paris Agreement as climate action lags: Lancet
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action

Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change .
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.

The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.

The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.

According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.

articles.title: Small fish: On Operation Trident
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: While carriers of narcotics are caught in the net, big sharks operate freely

Operation Trident , a multi-agency crackdown on an international syndicate operating across the India-Myanmar-Bangladesh corridor, marks a significant step-up in the government’s campaign against drug trafficking. The Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has set December 31, 2029, as the deadline to eradicate drug networks across the country. The October 23 raids, which led to 18 people being arrested , were based on NCB investigations following the arrest of an alleged Myanmar-based kingpin in Delhi this May. However, the dismantling of the entire network would require identification of all suppliers in Myanmar and their successful prosecution. The government’s strategy, involving States and Union Territories, over 40 Ministries, central agencies and the pharmaceutical sector, is outlined in the Vision Document on Drug Control (2026-2029), launched by Mr. Shah at the Narco-Coordination Centre meeting on June 26, 2026. It envisages dismantling 100 major cartels and improving prosecution outcomes. The broad strategy reflects the complexity of the problem and signals a more focused approach. Data for 2025 also show an increase of over 50% in arrests and a nearly 53% rise in cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act compared with 2024.

However, the government’s action-plan will depend on consistent implementation and efficient coordination among agencies, and striking at the real brains behind it all. In several cases, foreign-based key operatives still remain at large and big sharks often do not fall in the net. The 2021 Mundra port case in Gujarat, involving the seizure of about 3,000 kg of heroin, is a case in point wherein the principal Afghanistan-based suppliers have yet to be brought to book. Also, the quantity of drugs seized does not, by itself, indicate whether drug availability or consumption has declined. Punjab remains a prominent example of the continuing public health challenges associated with drug abuse. The alleged drug-related killings of anti-drug activists in Mansa and Gurdaspur, along with the alleged death by suicide of a father in Sangrur who had raised concerns about the easy availability of synthetic drugs in his locality, underscore the human cost of the problem. These incidents also raise questions about the protection of those who speak out against drug trafficking and networks. These concerns lend urgency to the objective of dismantling entire networks and apprehending the “big sharks”, rather than concentrating disproportionately on individual carriers. The key is to identify the ultimate beneficiaries by meticulously following the money trail and ensuring their conviction.

articles.title: Fouled waters: On Rajasthan’s river pollution
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: River pollution from industrial effluents indicates state failure

The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

The Court initiated a suo motu writ petition in 2025 and constituted a High-level Ecosystem Oversight Committee chaired by Justice Sangeet Lodha to audit the plants and draft a plan to restore the rivers. Based on the committee’s scathing status reports, Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta banned construction within 100 metres of the rivers’ edges and hazardous industries within 500 m of the present path, or of the flood lines where available. The Court has also upbraided local authorities for failing to enforce pollution norms by citing the Court’s own stay of a 2022 National Green Tribunal order imposing a compensation on the Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation and the local administration in Jodhpur and Barmer. The State regulatory apparatus has been dysfunctional: officials were aware of illegal mining operations in some areas, yet they regularised leases in those areas. Given the dereliction in play, the Court is correct to treat the possibility of collusion between State officials and industrial mafias seriously. Justice Mehta’s observation that the State could be held liable under the ‘polluter pays’ principle is also a significant indictment of state failure, through negligence. Now, importantly, the State still has to restore the Jojari and attend to its wellbeing, which is relevant to a recent tendency by the Court to substitute itself for regulators rather than disciplining them into discharging their functions. This needs to change.

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

River pollution from industrial effluents indicates state failure

The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

The Court initiated a suo motu writ petition in 2025 and constituted a High-level Ecosystem Oversight Committee chaired by Justice Sangeet Lodha to audit the plants and draft a plan to restore the rivers. Based on the committee’s scathing status reports, Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta banned construction within 100 metres of the rivers’ edges and hazardous industries within 500 m of the present path, or of the flood lines where available. The Court has also upbraided local authorities for failing to enforce pollution norms by citing the Court’s own stay of a 2022 National Green Tribunal order imposing a compensation on the Rajasthan State Industrial Development and Investment Corporation and the local administration in Jodhpur and Barmer. The State regulatory apparatus has been dysfunctional: officials were aware of illegal mining operations in some areas, yet they regularised leases in those areas. Given the dereliction in play, the Court is correct to treat the possibility of collusion between State officials and industrial mafias seriously. Justice Mehta’s observation that the State could be held liable under the ‘polluter pays’ principle is also a significant indictment of state failure, through negligence. Now, importantly, the State still has to restore the Jojari and attend to its wellbeing, which is relevant to a recent tendency by the Court to substitute itself for regulators rather than disciplining them into discharging their functions. This needs to change.

articles.title: Vedanta Group eyeing $20 billion profits over next two years: Chairman Anil Agarwal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Vedanta is targeting $11 billion in profits this year, Chairman Anil Agarwal said.
Vedanta Group is targeting revenue of $50 billion and profits of $20 billion over the next two years, founder and chairman Anil Agarwal said at an industry event in Kolkata.
“This year we would be making $30 billion revenue and $11 billion in profits. In two years, we would scale our revenues to $50 billion with $20 billion in profits,” he said.
The privately-owned diversified commodities producer has interests spanning aluminium, zinc, oil and gas, power, iron and steel, copper and other critical minerals.

Separately, its recently listed Vedanta Aluminium reported more than a doubling of net profit year-on-year to ₹6,187 crore for the quarter ended September. Revenue rose 41% to ₹22,066 crore during the period.
The company increased aluminium production by 5% year-on-year to 649 kilotonnes (KT). Production of value-added aluminium products rose 31% to 432 KT, while alumina output climbed 37% to 895 KT.

Vedanta Aluminium also reduced its net debt by ₹3,090 crore during the quarter compared with the preceding quarter, signalling an improvement in its debt position alongside higher production and earnings.

articles.title: The gap in manufacturing sector GVA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: According to the National Accounts Statistics, the manufacturing sector’s GVA is ₹38.6 lakh crore in 2023-24 at current prices.; however, an ‘Alternative Estimate’ using data from the Annual Survey of Industries and Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises gives a lower figure, prompting a closer look at the official estimate

Early this year, the National Statistical Office (NSO) released the new series of the National Accounts Statistics (NAS). It shows that the manufacturing sector’s gross value added (GVA) is ₹38.6 lakh crore (₹38.6 trillion), constituting 14.7 per cent of GDP (gross domestic product) for the year 2023-24 at current prices. How reliable is the official estimate? This article investigates.

The manufacturing sector has two parts: One comprises all registered factories employing 10+/20+ workers with/without power, including registered companies (defined as the organised/formal sector). The other comprises unincorporated/ informal/ household units consisting of small factories/workshops falling outside the corporate/factory sector. The Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) reports the production accounts of the factory sector, while the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE) covers the informal sector. The combined output (GVA) of the factory and unincorporated sectors almost completely represents total manufacturing output.

For 2023-24, the sum of the GVA of units covered by the ASI and ASUSE is ₹27.4 lakh crore (the Alternative Estimate or, AE). The official figure, as per the NAS, is ₹38.6 lakh crore. It is higher than the AE by a whopping 40.9 per cent. Let’s call this the GAP. What could account for it?

While minor variations between the two estimates is understandable due to methodological or definitional issues, such a substantial GAP between the two estimates using official data sources surely raises many questions.

What are the data sources used for estimating the official GVA? For the unincorporated sector, it is ASUSE – the same as what we have used to estimate the AE. Hence, it cannot account for the GAP noted above. Moreover, the unincorporated sector’s share in total manufacturing GVA is a mere 13.9 per cent.

Hence, the reason for the GAP must lie in the estimation of organised manufacturing output. The NAS uses company balance-sheet data sourced from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ database (MCA-21), compiled using the annual statutory filings by registered companies. This practice of using the MCA data began with the previous NAS revision (base year 2011-12), partially replacing the ASI. The procedure has continued in the latest revision, with minor modifications.

A standard way to validate the GVA is to use employment data to estimate the sector’s potential output by applying appropriate “technical ratios” drawn from the ASI and ASUSE datasets. The official Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for 2023-24, estimated that the manufacturing sector employed 697.5 lakh workers.

However, as per the ASI and ASUSE datasets, only 532.9 lakh workers were employed to produce the official GVA. Thus, quite possibly, the contribution of the remaining 164.6 lakh “residual workers” — 697.5 minus 532.9 — may account for the GAP in the GVA reported above.

The definitions of employment in the three surveys are not the same, and their data collection methods differ. However, for a validation exercise, the PLFS estimates provide a useful reference point. Official agencies also use similar methods.

Some of this GAP is contributed by the residual 2,72,534 MCA companies, not covered in the 78,618 “private companies” captured in the ASI data. A majority of the residual companies are likely to be to non-factory private companies. The left over residual workers are likely to belong to the unincorporated sector not covered in ASUSE survey because of their small size.

Under Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has vowed to topple Iran's government, the two countries have directly fought a war for the first time in their history after decades of enmity.

Tuesday's (October 27) pivotal election gave Israelis a chance to offer a verdict on Netanyahu's right-wing government, amid mounting U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran following their launch of the war in February.

"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X, referring to recent discussions at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.

Since the war erupted, it has severely disrupted energy shipments from Gulf countries after Iran began blockading the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.

In retaliation, the United States has been maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports, seeking to squeeze the country's economy.

But the newspaper, citing people briefed on the conversations, said President Donald Trump had not made a final decision.
Mr. Netanyahu, vying to form a coalition government after the closely contested polls, has said Israel has an opportunity to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.

articles.title: Netanyahu bloc leads Israel vote, falls short of majority
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: With more than three quarters of the vote counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc was slightly ahead but short of a majority

Results from Israel’s hard-fought election pointed on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) to no clear winner as a leader of the Arab minority appealed to a hesitant opposition to join forces to end the divisive reign of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

With more than three quarters of the vote counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc was slightly ahead but short of a majority in Tuesday’s (October 27, 2026) election, the first since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, which has led Israel to wage war on Gaza and across the region.

Both Mr. Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief leading a broad opposition bloc, vowed that they would seek to form the next government. But neither looks set to reach the 61-seat threshold for a majority. With 77% of ballots counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc had 54 of the 120 seats in Parliament and Mr. Eisenkot’s opposition had 49.
The results could still change but one place of clear gains was among Israeli Arab lists which were set to jump to 17 seats.

Voters from the Arab community, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after Israel’s creation and who make up around 20% of the population, have been enraged by the Netanyahu government’s ultra-nationalist Jewish vision for the country and the Palestinian territories.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the leftist Arab-majority Joint List, said the Israeli public had voted for new leadership, and “anyone who wants to offer a substantive and genuine alternative to Netanyahu’s blood-soaked government will have to talk to us”.
“It’s either the continuation of racism, the continuation of exclusion and the continuation of supremacy, or a genuine Jewish-Arab partnership,” he said.

Mr. Eisenkot has resisted allying with Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu during the campaign relentlessly attacked the opposition by saying it would put Arabs in power, running on the slogan: “Either the Right or Palestine.”
Yair Golan, the head of Israel’s main left-wing party and a member of Mr. Eisenkot’s camp, became the first member of the opposition camp to call for an alliance with Arab parties.
But Mr. Eisenkot’s camp also includes right-wingers who share many of Netanyahu’s hawkish views and have adamantly rejected working with Arab lawmakers.

articles.title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up 'very soon'
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: "There'll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made," Mr. Trump told reporters
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up "very soon."
The announcement came as Trump's administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
"There'll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made," Mr. Trump told reporters.
Mr. Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Mr. Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Mr. Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Mr. Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days, Mr. Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Mr. Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.

articles.title: India rejects patent bid for treatment of drug-resistant TB
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Civil society groups urge U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development to withdraw related patent claims in other countries

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.

“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.

The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.

The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.

The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.

India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.

“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.

In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.

articles.title: Vehicle data shared only in masked form: ULIP
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Clarification comes after Road Ministry sought audit of users accessing the Centre’s logistics portal following complaints that multiple apps and websites are selling vehicle information

After the Road Ministry sought an audit of users accessing the Centre’s logistics portal following complaints that multiple apps and websites were selling vehicle information, the Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP) rejected the allegations of its misuse. It said all data were masked and called for broader scrutiny of the platforms involved.

“ULIP relays information in the format received from the source API. For example, vehicle owner names, chassis and engine numbers retain their masking, and the mobile number field remains null in both the source response and the response provided to users. ULIP does not independently generate, unmask or enrich the underlying data,” ULIP wrote in response to a story in The Hindu .

The Road Ministry sought an audit after finding that some entities were extracting data in large volumes from ULIP with some as many pulling out as many as 50 lakh records a month. The Road Ministry shares vehicle information with multiple government agencies and private firms from its portals such as VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals.

ULIP says it uses sufficient safeguards that include screening of entities that have access to its portal, their proposed use cases, binding terms and conditions, IP whitelisting, phased onboarding and continuous monitoring of API usage. This framework complies with the Road Ministry’s Policy for Data Sharing from the National Transport Repository, which prescribes authentication, secret keys, masking of personally identifiable information (PII) and defined approval mechanisms, ULIP added.

Referring to multiple apps selling vehicle information data in unmasked form, ULIP said there needed to be a “scrutiny of wider ecosystem of platforms and channels through which such information is being made available”.

The Road Ministry has written to the government’s nodal agency for investigating cybersecurity incidents, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), seeking a forensic audit of VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals, which hold a range of vehicle-owner information.

It has also sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information and Technology (MEITY) for a review of its data sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it. The Road Ministry also plans to audit various enforcement agencies that access its portals for data.

The Ministry’s action follows reports that apps and websites were selling vehicle-linked personal data for as little as ₹5. A Cyderes investigation found that a Telegram-based broker could retrieve an owner’s name, contact details, addresses and other records from a vehicle registration number, along with driving licence, challan, FASTag and registration certificate information. The Ministry has asked major app-store operators, including Google, to remove such apps.

fullParagraphs: One in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body

Time is brain, when it comes to the treatment of strokes. But a stroke occurring during sleep may go unnoticed until a person wakes up with symptoms, leaving doctors without a clear timeline of its onset. This is where brain imaging helps doctors identify patients with wake-up strokes and assess the extent of injury to pave the way for prompt treatment. Neurologists underscore the need to seek medical care immediately to ensure timely treatment.

M. Radha, head of department and professor of neurology, Government Kilpauk Medical College (KMC) Hospital, Chennai, said that the prevalence of wake-up strokes is 20% - one in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body,” she said.

If a patient arrives at a hospital within 4.5 hours of stroke symptoms, then thrombolysis can be done, she said, adding: “However, in wake-up stroke, we cannot calculate the time of the onset of symptoms. We do not know the window. So, acting fast is important. In case of any symptoms, patients should reach the hospital on time.”

In wake-up strokes, imaging helps give a clear picture for the doctors. “An MRI brain scan should be taken immediately. If it is not available, a CT angiogram should be taken. The scans help us assess the extent of brain injury and blood flow to different parts of the brain. They can determine whether there is diffusion-perfusion mismatch. The difference may represent brain tissue that is still salvageable and can be potentially saved. Like in regular strokes, ‘time is brain’ in wake-up strokes too, making prompt diagnosis and treatment crucial,” she explained.

Shubha Subramanian, senior consultant - neurology, Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai, said that in ischemic strokes, thrombolysis is used to dissolve the blood clot if a patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. “In cases involving a large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is performed within 24 hours of symptom onset, depending on the patient’s eligibility. In wake-up strokes, we do not know when the stroke started; it could be at night or early in the morning. What we do next is crucial. This is why we rely on imaging techniques,” she added.

“MRI has a lot of sequences. If you compare the diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) imaging, a mismatch in that shows that the brain tissue is still salvageable. So even if we do not know the time of onset of stroke, we can still go ahead and thrombolyse the patient. In the same way, MRI perfusion or CT perfusion studies will also give us a clue regarding salvageable brain tissue. This will help us in taking crucial decisions regarding thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or whether to go for conservative management,” she elaborated.

Under the Tamil Nadu Accident and Emergency Care Initiative and Stroke Care and Rapid Intervention with Plasminogen activator and Thrombectomy (SCRIPT) programme implemented by the Tamil Nadu government and with facilities available at the new JICA building at KMC, patients with with wake-up strokes are regularly treated, Dr. Radha noted.

“There is effective coordination between the administration, the emergency department, radiology and neurology departments. We have a green channel in place. As a result, once the patients with symptoms of stroke enter the Emergency Department, the neurologist is intimated. Our doctor goes to the radiology department which has significantly reduced the door to needle time,” she said.

BE FAST is the acronym to spot the warning signs of stroke, denoting Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech and Time. “We do see that the awareness of stroke symptoms is increasing and the referral system has also improved,” Dr. Radha said.

Dr. Shubha Subramanian said that in wake-up strokes, the person may not realise that he/she has symptoms of stroke when they wake up from sleep. “They may face difficulty in getting up and may also fall as a result. It is important for family members to identify the symptoms and rush for medical help,” she added.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: The Supreme Court has pointed to the SIR’s flaws by design

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: At Wednesday’s hearing of a petition on the Delhi SIR in the Supreme Court, Justice Joymalya Bagchi asked questions that cut to the heart of the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s SIR of electoral rolls . If an existing voter was “lax, inert or did not respond” to enumeration forms, was that a ground for the ECI to “forfeit his or her right to vote forever”? The Bench headed by the Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said that the ECI was in “error” to force such voters, struck off for not returning enumeration forms, to reapply on Form 6 as if they were new voters. It asked why voters who had shifted residences could not just disclose details and why deleted voters could not fill enumeration forms belatedly. This is the central design flaw of the SIR as it shifts the burden of enrolment from the state to the elector, including those who have voted before, and treats a mere change of address as ground for deletion. The share of draft deletions recorded as “shifted” or “absent” rose from 55% in Bihar to 72% in States/Union Territories in Phase 3. In Karnataka, about 84 lakh electors were deleted, marked as “shifted” or “absent” during enumeration. But only a net of 8.2 lakh, including new electors, were added during the claims phase, with the final roll being 64.5 lakh short of the projected adult population. Requiring moved voters to re-register as fresh applicants defeats the ECI’s historic mandate of widening the franchise, which was inherent in the 2002-03 intensive revision, where enumerators enrolled shifted voters at their new homes and the Chief Electoral Officer reconciled the old entries.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: court / Election Commission of India / Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls / voting / Delhi / Karnataka / Bihar / West Bengal / minority group

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: Public functionaries must not use privacy to seek exemption from scrutiny

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Digital News Publishers Association’s (DNPA) challenge to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 , and its Rules , has drawn attention to concerns that a law to safeguard informational privacy risks creating a serious chilling effect on the media. The absence of a specific exemption for journalistic activity could subject reporters investigating official misconduct or corruption to the obligations of a “data fiduciary”, requiring them to notify and seek consent from the very individuals they are investigating. Such onerous requirements could affect investigations undertaken in the public interest. The implications extend to routine newsgathering too, where personal information is integral to reporting. The omission is particularly consequential because the drafts in 2018, 2019 and 2021 carried a journalistic exemption. The Act already provides exemptions for certain forms of data processing, including for research and statistical purposes, making the denial of similar protection to journalists difficult to justify. Non-compliance can attract penalties of up to ₹250 crore, posing an existential threat to smaller and independent newsrooms. The DNPA petition also challenges Section 44(3), which amended the RTI Act, 2005, removing the earlier public-interest qualification concerning disclosure of personal information. The protection of personal information must not be absolute; an overriding public interest must remain a legitimate ground for disclosure, particularly when the information is held by public authorities. Investigations into corruption often rely on asset disclosures and tender documents containing personal data. Restricting access to these records risks reducing journalism to merely reproducing government releases.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: data protection / law / online / media / investigation / Right to Information / court / social media / ministers (government)

This particular rapidity is a challenge for forecasters and some models did fail to anticipate how strong Arnab would become. It also moved faster than expected towards the coast, before stalling for a time and beginning the landfall process several hours before the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted it would, in the middle of the night, leaving many district authorities with a potentially narrower window to evacuate high-risk settlements. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: Operation Trident , a multi-agency crackdown on an international syndicate operating across the India-Myanmar-Bangladesh corridor, marks a significant step-up in the government’s campaign against drug trafficking. The Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has set December 31, 2029, as the deadline to eradicate drug networks across the country. The October 23 raids, which led to 18 people being arrested , were based on NCB investigations following the arrest of an alleged Myanmar-based kingpin in Delhi this May. However, the dismantling of the entire network would require identification of all suppliers in Myanmar and their successful prosecution. The government’s strategy, involving States and Union Territories, over 40 Ministries, central agencies and the pharmaceutical sector, is outlined in the Vision Document on Drug Control (2026-2029), launched by Mr. Shah at the Narco-Coordination Centre meeting on June 26, 2026. It envisages dismantling 100 major cartels and improving prosecution outcomes. The broad strategy reflects the complexity of the problem and signals a more focused approach. Data for 2025 also show an increase of over 50% in arrests and a nearly 53% rise in cases registered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act compared with 2024.

dailyQuiz10.explanation:
1. Core Context & Background: River pollution from industrial effluents indicates state failure

2. Constitutional / Economic / Policy Analysis: The Supreme Court has pulled up, once again, the Rajasthan government over industrial effluents flowing into the Jojari river and the deadly risk it poses for the people depending on it. The problem is decades old — public interest litigation in the Rajasthan High Court alerted State machinery to the problem in 2011 — indicating an oversight by the State bordering on the systematic. The Jojari, the Luni, and the Bandi are seasonal rivers in the State’s arid western region, flowing through Jodhpur, Balotra, and Pali districts. This region has also evolved as a textile-dyeing and steelworking hub, and untreated or insufficiently treated effluents from these factories have run directly into the rivers and soil, endangering the health of around 20 lakh local residents. The region also suffers rampant illegal sand mining in riverbeds. The sewage treatment plants have been able to accommodate only around half of the sewage generated in the three urban centres, according to the State’s submissions to the Court in 2025, even as the Court recorded substantial underutilisation at common effluent treatment plants. The combination is suggestive of industrial sources bypassing treatment facilities, poor connections between the sources and the facilities, and/or insufficient capacity at particular sites or in specific periods.

3. Way Forward & Exam Conclusion: court / Rajasthan / water pollution / rivers / pollution control / textile and clothing / iron and steel / health
